questions.stem:
A law was passed in 1919 that gave the government enormous powers to repress political activities and allowed detention of political prisoners without trial for two years. It had been hurriedly passed despite the united opposition of the Indian members. Mahatma Gandhi decided to launch a nationwide satyagraha against it. He wanted non-violent civil disobedience, and the movement was to begin with a hartal on 6 April. Rallies were organised in various cities, workers went on strike in railway workshops, and shops closed down. Alarmed by the popular upsurge, and scared that lines of communication such as the railways and telegraph would be disrupted, the British administration decided to clamp down on nationalists.

Read the case and answer the three questions below, each in one or two lines. (i) What two harsh powers did the law of 1919 hand to the government? (ii) Name the three forms the protest took in the towns. (iii) A trader complains that the hartal and the strikes were only a nuisance to business; explain why the administration nevertheless treated the movement as a threat.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Powers to repress political activities, and detention of political prisoners without trial for two years. (ii) Rallies in various cities, strikes in railway workshops, and shops closing down. (iii) The upsurge was popular and could disrupt the railways and telegraph, so the administration clamped down.

On 10 April the police in Amritsar fired upon a peaceful procession, provoking widespread attacks on banks, post offices and railway stations. Martial law was imposed and General Dyer took command. On 13 April the infamous Jallianwalla Bagh incident took place. A large crowd had gathered in the enclosed ground; some had come to protest the government's new repressive measures, while others had come to attend the annual Baisakhi fair. Being from outside the city, many villagers were unaware of the martial law that had been imposed. Dyer entered the area, blocked the exit points, and opened fire on the crowd, killing hundreds.

Read the case and answer the three questions below, each in one or two lines. (i) What provoked the attacks on banks, post offices and railway stations? (ii) Why had the crowd gathered in the enclosed ground, and what did many of them not know? (iii) A historian notes that Dyer later declared the object of his action; state what that object was and what it reveals about his intention.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) The police firing on a peaceful procession on 10 April. (ii) Some came to protest the new repressive measures, others to attend the annual Baisakhi fair; many villagers did not know martial law had been imposed. (iii) His object was to produce a moral effect, creating terror and awe in the minds of satyagrahis.

questions.stem:
As the news of Jallianwalla Bagh spread, crowds took to the streets in many north Indian towns. There were strikes, clashes with the police and attacks on government buildings. The government responded with brutal repression, seeking to humiliate and terrorise people: satyagrahis were forced to rub their noses on the ground, crawl on the streets, and do salaam to all sahibs; people were flogged and villages around Gujranwala in Punjab were bombed. Seeing violence spread, Mahatma Gandhi called off the movement. While the Rowlatt satyagraha had been a widespread movement, it was still limited mostly to cities and towns. Gandhi now felt the need to launch a more broad-based movement in India, but was certain that none could be organised without bringing Hindus and Muslims closer together.

Read the case and answer the three questions below, each in one or two lines. (i) Name two forms of humiliation the government forced on satyagrahis. (ii) Why did Gandhi call the movement off, and what limit had he noticed in it? (iii) A student observes that the protests were strongest in towns; explain what this shows about the movement's reach, and what Gandhi believed had to be brought about before any broader movement could be organised.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Rubbing their noses on the ground, crawling on the streets, and salaam to all sahibs. (ii) Violence was spreading, and the movement stayed mostly in cities and towns. (iii) Its reach was limited; Gandhi believed Hindus and Muslims had to be brought closer together before a broad-based movement could be organised.
